summary: Specifies the Diameter base protocol, a framework for authentication, authorization, and accounting for uses such as network access and IP mobility, in both local and roaming situations. It defines the message format, transport, error handling, and security. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 6733.

plainLanguage.summary: Diameter is a framework for systems that check a user's identity, decide what service is allowed, and record usage. This RFC defines the shared message, connection, routing, error, session, accounting, and security rules that Diameter applications build on.

subtitle: A base protocol for authentication, authorization, accounting, and application messages.

tldr.problem: Network access and mobility services need a common way for systems to exchange authentication, authorization, and accounting information.
tldr.mechanism: Diameter defines request and answer messages, attribute-value pairs, peer connections, routing, error handling, sessions, and security requirements.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3588 was obsoleted by RFC 6733, which replaced the Diameter base protocol specification.

today: RFC 3588 was obsoleted by RFC 6733, which replaced this Diameter base protocol specification.

sections.title: A Shared AAA Framework
sections.content:
Authentication checks identity, authorization determines permitted actions, and accounting records service use. The Diameter base protocol supplies common rules for these tasks in network access and IP mobility, including local and roaming settings.

Applications define which commands and attributes they need. The base protocol handles common message exchange and peer behavior, while authentication and authorization use is extended by application specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Diameter gives network services a shared way to ask who a user is, what the user may do, and what service was used. Specific applications add their own request details.

sections.title: Messages and Attribute-Value Pairs
sections.content:
A Diameter message has a header followed by attribute-value pairs (AVPs). The header identifies the command and application, distinguishes a request from an answer, and carries identifiers used to match replies and detect duplicates.

AVPs hold information such as identity, routing, accounting, and security data. Each AVP has a code, flags, a length, and data; a vendor identifier can mark a vendor-specific AVP. Mandatory flags tell a receiver whether an unknown value requires rejecting the message.
sections.plainLanguage: A Diameter message has a header and a set of named data items called AVPs. The header describes the request or answer, and the AVPs carry the information the application needs.

sections.title: Peers, Connections, and Agents
sections.content:
Diameter peers establish transport connections, exchange capabilities, and can detect failures and reconnect. The base protocol uses TCP or SCTP on port 3868; nodes must secure Diameter traffic with TLS or IPsec.

Agents can relay or proxy requests, redirect a sender to another server, or translate between protocols. A connection is the transport link between two peers; a session is an application-level interaction identified by a Session-Id and can span messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers use a protected transport connection to exchange Diameter messages. Agents can forward or redirect requests, while a session keeps track of one user's application-level service.

sections.title: Routing, Sessions, and Accounting
sections.content:
Requests identify their origin and destination so a node can process them locally or send them toward another realm or server. Answers return result information, while defined error codes and AVPs describe protocol failures and unsuccessful requests.

Session procedures cover authorization, reauthorization, termination, and aborting a service. Accounting messages report events and records, and applications define which session and accounting details apply to their service.
sections.plainLanguage: Diameter routes requests to the right server and returns an answer with a result. It also defines how applications track service sessions and report accounting events.

sections.title: Security and Replacement
sections.content:
The base protocol requires a security mechanism and prohibits using Diameter without TLS or IPsec. The RFC also discusses peer-to-peer security and the use of those protections across different network boundaries.

RFC 3588 was published as a Proposed Standard and later obsoleted by RFC 6733. Its base message and application framework should therefore be read as the earlier Diameter specification, not the replacement text.
sections.plainLanguage: Diameter messages must use TLS or IPsec; the RFC does not permit unprotected Diameter connections. RFC 6733 later replaced this version of the base protocol.
